newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundesbank signals policy on hold for now.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank signals policy on hold for now.

text.p: Bu Janet Northcote
The Bundesbank on Tuesday signalled that its monetary policy remained on hold, defying market speculation that it would signal an interest rate tightening to support the mark against the dollar.

The central bank called for bids for securities repurchase funds at an unchanged interest rate of three percent, in line with an announcement it had made following the last meeting of its policy-making council on July 24.
Financial markets had speculated that the central bank could make a further announcement when it set this week's regular repo pact, possibly offering a second set of funds under different conditions.

A decision to set a second securities repurchase pact at variable interest rates -- where banks bid for funds at the interest rates of their choosing -- would have been seen as a signal that the central bank was prepared to let interest rates drift higher.
Speculation of such a move is likely to persist at least until next week, when the central bank will be calling for bids for money market funds at conditions which have not yet been announced.

Talk that the central bank -- which has been following an easing policy since 1992 -- could move back into tightening mode was triggered almost two weeks ago, when the central bank made clear it was leaving its policy options open for the second half of its four-week summer holiday break.

Deviating from the pattern recently established, the Bundesbank announced that its repo rate would remain steady for the first two weeks of the holiday but made no comment on its plans for the second half of the period.

This prompted talk that the bank could be planning a tightening during the holiday period, although some analysts said the central bank could simply be signalling that it remained active even when no council meetings were scheduled.
The sharp slide in the mark, and surging prices on Germany's equities market, have been judged by some as sufficiently unsettling to spur the Bundesbank to action.
The focus now will shift to August 12, when the next tender is due to be announced.
Although the Bundesbank could theoretically make an announcement on its plans for next week's repo at any stage, most analysts believe it will wait until the regular announcement time.
At that stage the central bank will have four main options.
-- It could set a further fixed rate tender at an unchanged three percent rate.
-- It could set a tender at variable interest rates.
-- It could set a "double decker" tender, offering some funds at a fixed interest rate and some at variable rates.
-- Or it could set a new fixed rate tender at a different interest rate from the three percent which has now prevailed for about a year, most likely nudging the rate higher.

The central bank could also signal a tightening by simply draining liquidity from the market, pushing up rates by increasing the scarcity of funds. It could also mop up liquidity using exchange rate swaps or other means.
Any action will be decided by the central bank's Frankfurt-based directorate on the basis of guidelines given by the Bundesbank council at its last meeting. Those guidelines are shrouded in secrecy.
